newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Power firms decry Pakistani wavering on agreements.
newsitem.headline: Power firms decry Pakistani wavering on agreements.

text.p: Any move by Pakistan to force private power firms to revise agreed tariffs could scare off foreign investors, industry sources and stocks analysts say.
"The power tariffs reflect the going rate. It's not in their (Pakistan's) interest to renegotiate them. We would all run away, wouldn't we?" said one foreign fund manager.

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif last month ordered a committee to be set up to study power purchase agreements signed by the former government led by Benazir Bhutto with a view to persuading a score of power companies to reduce agreed tariffs.
The tariff review committee is expected to submit its report to the government by the end of this month.
"The government has not chosen the appropriate way of going about this issue," said a consultant for a U.S.-based company with power projects in Pakistan. He asked not to be identified.

"I do not see any ground for a renegotiation," Mike Woodroffe, chief executive of Hub Power Co, told Reuters. He said power rates could only be reduced if the committee found a way to cut the cost of running a power plant.
Hub Power's 1,292-megawatt capacity plant in the coastal industrial estate of Hub west of Karachi, has been selling power to the Water and Power Development Authority since June 1996.
Woodroffe said he hoped that once Pakistan's economy picked up, the government would realise the tariffs were good value.

The consultant said uncertainty about government policy and media speculation that tariffs and project costs had been inflated could do more damage than any actual revision because they cast a question mark over Pakistan's ability to handle policies drawn up specifically to attract foreign investment.

"If the government had some problems raising cash for buying the power they could simply have approached us. But forcing power companies to lower tariffs through threats and allegations is not the right approach," he said.

Credit Lyonnais Securities Asia said in a research note this week that talk of renegotiation had clouded the realisation of returns earlier thought guaranteed, raising the risk premium for all private power companies, including Hub Power Co.

Bhutto's government, eager to woo foreign investment, issued letters of support between 1994 and 1996 for new plants with a total capacity of almost 3,000 MW at a guaranteed payment of $0.065 per kilowatt-hour for the first 10 years. Most of these projects are due to come onstream by the end of 1998.
An official at the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority said tariffs had to be revised because buying power from the new plants would cost some $1.6 billion a year.

"What the government actually wants is to do away with the higher tariffs in the first two years of operation and smooth out payments by maintaining an average tariff over the 25-year life of these power plants," he said.

The power policy unveiled in 1994 offered private power projects $0.0833 per kwh in the first year of operation and $0.0666 per kwh in the second, an average of $0.065 per kwh for the first 10 years and $0.0591 over the life of the projects.
The official said the government favoured changing this structure to a flat $0.059 per kwh over the life of the project.
"Roughly 35 percent of the tariff comprises fuel charges, 35 percent is debt repayments and the rest is for operating cost," said the consultant. "Where would they like us to cut back?"
He said tariffs could only be cut substantially if the government pared taxes and duties on imports of fuel and spares.
"If Malaysia, with a much lower risk profile, is offering $0.062 (per kwh), Pakistan should be happy with the $0.065 rate as its risk profile is much higher," he said.
